Run the experiments in this order

IDControlled experiment and mechanismRequired observations and decision
D01 — exact target and protocolQualify target-only on the four-GPU vLLM baseline and SGLang TP4 control. Start with short requests and low load, then run the scored suites.Save load/repacking/graph memory, actual kernels, effective C4/C128 state dtype/pool capacities and all encoding/parser settings. Compare to the publisher reference on supported diagnostic cases; use declared numerical tolerances if logits are available, and scored outcomes otherwise. Stop before timing on unexplained fallback, invalid outputs or tool/reasoning boundary failures.
D02 — compressed history and indexer precisionWith target-only and topology fixed, compare the qualified default/higher-precision indexer cache with the supported FP4 indexer path. Hold MLA KV and C4/C128 compressed-state dtype fixed; vary each only in a separately qualified experiment.Log the effective indexer representation, attention backend and memory pools. Score long-context tasks and move evidence across the 128-token recent-window boundary and the installed cache-page boundaries. Include chunked prefill, prefix reuse, eviction and cancellation. A lower memory figure is insufficient if retrieval or answer quality regresses.
D03 — four versus eight GPUsFirst measure one qualified four-GPU group. Then compare one DP8+EP group with two independent DP4+EP groups on the same eight-GPU node, if both qualify. Evaluate SGLang TP4/TP8 and two TP4 groups as separate qualified candidates.Hold aggregate admission/concurrency and prefix-routing policy fixed for the first comparison; tune separately. Record per-group queues, all GPU/CPU resources, per-rank memory and expert/communication imbalance. Report whole-node goodput and tails under the same offered workload. A four-versus-eight scaling result alone cannot rank equal-cost deployments.
D04 — natural DSparkOn the same qualified topology/cache settings, compare no DSpark with the engine's documented DSpark default. SGLang starts at five proposals; its documented downward sweep is 1–5. vLLM's recipe starts at seven; vary supported proposal counts separately.Record proposed, accepted and emitted tokens, draft/verify time, graphs and memory, queueing, final-answer latency and quality. Exercise accepted/rejected blocks, stop/EOS inside a block, cancellation, cache churn and the next session. No simulated acceptance. Do not equate the checkpoint's block size, CLI proposal count and tokens emitted after verification.
D05 — effort and output budgetWithin a qualified serving configuration, compare application-selected low/high/max reasoning budgets on the same tasks; keep those settings fixed for engine A/B.Score useful final answers and record first-final-answer latency, generated reasoning/answer tokens, output-limit finishes and elapsed time. Treat short-budget results as budget-constrained measurements, not reproductions of the publisher's high/max evaluation.
D06 — scheduling under mixed loadReplay short chat/tools, long documents and long coding generations. Vary one supported admission, prefill-chunk or graph setting, then confirm the selected combination.Measure offered/completed/scored requests, queue delay, TTFT, first-answer/end-to-end tails, failures and node goodput. Repeat with cache eviction and burst recovery. Retain all failed runs and check that the client or tool harness is not the bottleneck.

The recipe's FP4 indexer cache is a separate option from native FP4 expert storage. Inspect the installed build's actual flag and default before D02; omitting a flag is not evidence that an optimization is off. If changing precision also changes a kernel, label the result as that paired change. Do not transplant sparse-attention optimizations for another DeepSeek release without exact 0731 evidence. deepseek-v4-flash-0731-VR.

The SGLang family cookbook separately documents SGLANG_DSV4_COMPRESS_STATE_DTYPE for C4/C128 state pools: it describes FP32 as the default and a BF16 offline-compression option that can change automatic pool capacity. Its example names the earlier DeepSeek-V4-Flash, so this is a reason to inspect and record the exact 0731 build's effective state dtype, not evidence that the BF16 option qualifies for 0731. Qualify that path separately before a state-precision experiment and keep allocated capacity fixed before testing any capacity gain. deepseek-v4-flash-0731-GR.

For D04, the publisher vLLM example uses greedy drafting while the local recipe/profile uses probabilistic drafting. Keep client sampling fixed and record the draft sampling/rejection policy; these are different candidate configurations. SGLang's documented default verifies six positions for five proposals. Start from the documented settings and qualify changes; do not modify model config to make the numbers match. Publisher card, SGLang DSpark guidance.

Length and load are constrained experiments

Start with 4K/16K/32K serialized inputs, concurrency 1 and 8, then 32 and a fixed offered-rate ladder around saturation. Here K means 1,024 tokens. Include a near-cap bucket only after reserving generation, tool schema and history tokens inside the 65,536-token profile limit. A 64K input with any output is infeasible in these profiles. Raising the cap for 64K/128K inputs requires a separate load/memory/quality pass; the configured 1M positional ceiling is not a capacity result.

Short 128/1,024-token output caps are useful for shape diagnostics, but may censor reasoning before an answer. For scored quality, choose the budget using a separate pilot and record truncated or missing-final-answer cases rather than discarding them. The publisher recommends up to 384K output for high/max effort; that cannot fit the local cap, and any long-output arm must reserve the prompt in addition to output. Report application budget results as such. The publisher's sampling guidance also differs between agentic and other work, so freeze the selected policy for every A/B comparison. Usage guidance.

Separate export follow-up

Fresh cookbook research also identified nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-NVFP4 at f1caa71142bd0be02f728c79f75042ac1e461579. Its immutable card names this exact base release and states that DSpark heads were preserved but speculation was not exercised in its release validation. It is distinct from the preview-family NVFP4 checkpoint. deepseek-v4-flash-0731-NV-CARD.

This is an unqualified additional arm, with no atlas launch profile. Before adding it, audit its tensor/scaling map, exclusions, exact loader/backend, terms and image, then compare target-only native versus this export on the same qualified topology and effective cache settings. Run the scored coding/tool/long-context suites before spending any saved capacity or adding DSpark. Do not convert the publisher's quality table or the presence of draft tensors into a local quality/speed claim. The current native catalog/profile records remain the identity for D01–D06.

Produce a decision with its limits

The base card's code-agent results use the publisher's named harness and max-effort settings; the card describes that harness as pending release. Its internal DSBench scores are not reproducible local acceptance gates. The SGLang four-GB300 example establishes an upstream configuration report, not a measurement on this B300 node. The unresolved 284B-versus-304B accounting must not be used as a substitute for loaded tensor bytes or measured memory. Publisher card, architecture accounting.

For every candidate, retain exact model/build/encoding identities, benchmark/adapter/scorer manifests, raw answers and tool traces, per-item scores, paired uncertainty, truncation/error counts, cache/acceptance diagnostics, per-rank peak memory and whole-node latency/goodput. Join task success and timing by request ID if reporting quality-adjusted goodput. The atlas streaming probe does not save answers or run a tool loop and cannot supply that evaluation by itself.

Promote only when predeclared critical-task quality margins and service objectives pass across repeated runs. Reject demonstrated correctness or service regressions, mark missing support/adapter requirements blocked, and mark insufficient evidence inconclusive. There is no invented SLA, score target or “fastest engine” conclusion in this plan.

Remaining uncertainty

Exact main-plus-draft parameter accounting; selected image and kernel provenance; local B300 capacity, throughput and application correctness; qualification of eight-GPU adaptations.

Use the result schema for probe records and the experiment/quality manifests for scored campaigns. Empty results mean not measured. Preserve failed runs and the qualified baseline for rollback.

companies/google/gemma-4-31b-it/architecture.md

Gemma 4 31B IT: architecture

Data flow

Vision/text → [five local sliding layers → one global layer] ×10 with dense MLPs → tied output head + logit soft-cap → sampling.

How the parts work together

Five local sliding-attention layers are followed by one global layer. Local attention keeps recent context within a bounded window, while global layers provide long-distance interaction. This substantially changes the cache shape relative to 60 uniform full-attention layers.

Local and global attention have different KV-head counts and head dimensions. The publisher describes unified keys and values in the global layers. This same-layer behavior is distinct from the configuration’s num_kv_shared_layers: 0. A formula that allocates separate K and V buffers in every layer is therefore an assumption about storage, not a deduction from the config. Inspect the selected engine’s allocator before claiming an exact physical cache size.

The feed-forward blocks are dense and use the configured GELU approximation. Tied embeddings and output-head behavior matter both for loading and for quantization exclusions. Final logit soft-capping changes how scores reach the sampler; it must remain in the generation path.

Image features are processed through the vision tower before text generation. The presence of audio token identifiers elsewhere in a shared family configuration is not proof of an audio encoder in this specific variant. Capability must be checked at the concrete model, processor and runtime level.

The architecture facts above are drawn from the publisher card and configuration; the workload consequences are analytical interpretation. gemma-4-31b-it-CARD gemma-4-31b-it-CFG

This is a selected, normalized projection, not a byte-for-byte copy of the complete config. Field labels have been made comparable across models. Layer indices explicitly state zero-based or one-based conventions.

Memory and performance consequences

The pinned base repository lists 62,546,338,248 bytes of BF16 safetensors files, including file headers (about 62.55 decimal GB). This weight magnitude makes TP1 a reasonable B300 candidate; actual startup headroom still needs measuring. The rounded 31B family label is not an exact tensor census. gemma-4-31b-it-BASE-TREE

Lower precision can free memory for more requests or longer inputs. Multiple TP1 replicas use separate GPUs and separate weight copies; they do not create extra GPUs. Compare their aggregate throughput and per-request latency with tensor sharding under the same node budget.

Local and global cache pools need compatible budgeting. A user who sends many maximum-length requests can exhaust global cache even though most layers use a short window. Vision preprocessing adds its own transient memory; count image size and number, not merely the number of HTTP requests.

Repository file metadata and any cache calculations are not measured GPU allocations. Memory mathematics explains the formulas and their limits. gemma-4-31b-it-CARD gemma-4-31b-it-CFG HW

The public artifacts do not disclose every training-data, optimization or implementation detail. This report does not fill missing details with assumptions or present a complete formal reconstruction of private training.

Gemma 4 31B IT: serving on 8×B300

Status: unbenchmarked local recommendations. The upstream recipes are evidence of documented support, not a benchmark of your node.

Engine and topology

Start with vLLM TP1, 32K context and restrained concurrency. Compare BF16, RedHat block FP8 and RedHat NVFP4. The exact tool template is a versioned deployment asset, not a path guaranteed to exist inside every image; the baseline profile therefore does not blindly reference a source-tree-relative example file.

SGLang is an alternative to qualify for the exact export. The generic Hugging Face “use with SGLang” widget does not establish that a particular quantization format works in the selected image. A profile marked compatibility-probe must first load and pass protocol/accuracy tests.

Keep audio disabled for this variant unless a separately verified processor/runtime path proves the intended capability. Do not copy the generic example’s audio limit and advertise audio support.

gemma-4-31b-it-CARD HW

Experiment sequence

Compare TP1 BF16/FP8/NVFP4 at matched context and batch; verify global/local cache accounting; test thinking on/off separately; include image grounding, tool-call JSON, long-distance retrieval and concurrent cancellations.

First capture actual GPU memory, compute capability, peer topology and software versions with python scripts/preflight.py. Then resolve immutable model metadata, inspect the rendered profile and run the target-only correctness suite. Profiles live in profiles.

Acceptance gates

A successful load is necessary but insufficient. Require valid streaming framing, finite outputs, correctly separated reasoning, valid tool calls where supported, repeatable quality tests, bounded memory at load, and correct cache/state behavior after cancellation. Only then compare latency and throughput.

For production, place one sharded model process group inside a pod that owns its whole GPU group. Do not make eight independent KServe replicas and expect them to form TP8. Start with colocated prefill and decode; adopt disaggregation only after it wins the workload comparison and state transfer is correct. KS KSLLM

Parameters are not magic constants

The profile’s context cap is an application policy. Tensor parallelism is a starting layout. Memory utilization reserves room for non-weight allocations; changing it can trade cache space against startup headroom. Batch-token and sequence caps trade prefill efficiency against memory and queueing. Speculative depth trades draft/verification cost against naturally accepted tokens. Each must be varied one at a time before interaction testing.

Remaining uncertainty

Physical KV allocation under attention_k_eq_v in the selected engine; exact export-level SGLang compatibility; correct tool template at the final image revision; local B300 quality and latency.

Gemma 4 31B IT: validation ledger

CheckStatus in this ZIP
Publisher identity and named base repositoryRechecked 2026-10-15 against the pinned publisher card

Decision and applicability

Proposed experiments; no GPU results. Select the export and GPU grouping for a text/image service with a measured quality floor. Gemma's 50 sliding-attention layers, ten global layers, tied embeddings/head and final logit soft-cap require more specific checks than a uniform dense-transformer throughput sweep. The base and both Red Hat current cards/configs matched the atlas pins on 2026-10-15 UTC. gemma-4-31b-it-CFG, architecture.

Start with vLLM BF16 TP1, then the pinned FP8 and NVFP4 exports. The SGLang NVFP4 profile remains an exact-export compatibility probe. Require evidence that the selected build handles compressed-tensors block FP8 or packed NVFP4, as applicable, before timing. Resolve effective KV dtype rather than inferring it from weight precision. The exports preserve some components at higher precision; their file-size ratios do not predict GPU-memory or speed ratios. precision.

The supplied profiles allow 32,768 total tokens and 32 active requests. Screen 4K/16K serialized inputs with 128/1,024 output-token budgets at concurrency 1 and 8, then 32 if qualified. Account for image and template tokens. Longer contexts, larger batches and additional replicas require separate capacity checks. Audio is excluded for this variant (audio_config: null); a generic family example does not qualify it. The profiles intentionally omit automatic tools: pin the Gemma template/parser and verify its behavior before tool evaluation. No matching drafter is identified in these profiles, so a speculative-decoding claim for another Gemma variant is not an experiment ready to run here. gemma-4-31b-it-CARD.

Architecture and export experiments

ID / hypothesisControlled experimentEvidence and decision
G31-01 — Text quantization retains useful text and image quality.Compare BF16, block FP8 and NVFP4 in one qualified vLLM build at TP1 and matched KV dtype, cache policy, mode and batch. Verify loaded exclusions, tied embedding/head handling and the configured soft-cap; compare finite outputs with the publisher reference. Repeat the same export in SGLang only after its load gate.Save effective module/backend diagnostics, startup/repacking peak, steady memory and task-specific quality deltas. Report text and multimodal results separately: keeping vision weights at higher precision does not guarantee image-conditioned language quality. Stop on loader mismatches, unintended fallback or quality failure.
G31-02 — Sliding/global attention remains correct across cache boundaries.Place known facts just inside and outside the 1,024-token local window and at early/middle/late positions in longer prompts. Compare cold prefill, chunked prefill and warm-prefix replay where supported. Add divergent suffixes, eviction, batch-size changes and cancellation, then replay from a fresh session.Collect local/global pool occupancy, allocator block sizes, evictions and task-by-position accuracy. Facts outside the local window still have a global path; distinguish ordinary model errors from a repeatable cache-policy regression against the fresh reference. Do not infer physical K/V buffer sharing solely from attention_k_eq_v.
G31-03 — Document resolution buys enough accuracy to justify its cost.Freeze processor revision, source image bytes, aspect ratio handling and prompt. Start with one page; vary page count and resolution in separate experiments within the verified processor limits. Repeat identical text with different images and reversed page order. Add ordered video-frame inputs only after that exact processor/runtime path qualifies.Report text/table/formula errors, visual-token counts, preprocessing/encoder time where available, TTFT, peak memory and completion failures. Missing/reordered images or reused results from another image reject the path. Document accuracy cannot establish temporal-video accuracy, and frame input does not qualify an arbitrary video API.
G31-04 — Thinking and tool handling preserve the user-visible contract.Freeze thinking on/off within each export/engine A/B, with explicit output budgets and sampling. Separately compare thinking policies on identical tasks. After parser qualification, test no-call, single-call, multiple-call and multi-turn tool results, including streaming boundaries and cancellations.Save parsed reasoning, final answers and tool calls with their raw streams. Measure first-answer latency and task correctness, not only TTFT or valid JSON. A malformed parser output is a protocol failure; a well-formed wrong function is a quality failure.
G31-05 — Replicas improve node capacity more than tensor sharding.Compare eight TP1 replicas, four TP2 groups and two TP4 groups on the same eight GPUs for the same qualified export. Reuse an arrival trace containing short chat, long documents and image requests, with fixed routing/cache affinity and CPU resources. Fix total-node admission/concurrency and log per-group batching/scheduler limits before separate capacity tuning.Report whole-node goodput under declared latency/quality requirements, tails, per-GPU peak/headroom and burst recovery. Changed admission or batching policies require a complete-configuration comparison. Keep single-group latency separate. If image preprocessing saturates CPU or a global cache pool fills first, document that bottleneck before changing TP.

The source configuration motivates these cases; the expected performance outcome remains unknown. Lower precision, more replicas and a larger window are choices to evaluate independently before interaction testing. gemma-4-31b-it-CFG, serving.

Quality tasks chosen for this model

Task and primary sourceWhy it belongs here / controls and outputs
OmniDocBench v1.5 — MBENCH-OMNIDOC-V15Document parsing directly exercises variable-resolution vision and long generated structure. Pin the v1.5 code and matching dataset revisions, image policy, prompt and matching configuration. Report text/read-order edit distance, table TEDS and formula CDM separately. The publisher names v1.5; current main has later revisions. Its stated average edit distance is not interchangeable with the benchmark's composite overall score.
MMMU-Pro — MBENCH-MMMUPROUse a fixed standard or vision setting to check image-dependent reasoning beyond transcription. Preserve image-placeholder order and pin prompt mode; report per-subject accuracy and failures. This complements document parsing because correct OCR can still lead to a wrong answer.
RULER v1 — MBENCH-RULER-V1Use fixed generated retrieval, tracing and aggregation tasks to examine the local/global attention tradeoff at feasible lengths. Pin both its driver and linked NeMo-Skills implementation; report per-task/length scores. Keep the custom 1,024-token boundary probes outside the standard benchmark aggregate.
LiveCodeBench — MBENCH-LCBA frozen release_v6 or declared date window gives executable checks of thinking and quantization during long code generation. Pin evaluator limits, prompt adapter and samples per problem; report pass@1, truncation and runtime errors. This tests coding quality, without establishing an agent's repository-editing success.
BFCL — MBENCH-BFCLUse declared offline single/multi-turn categories only after the Gemma parser/template gate. Measure selected function and arguments, including no-call cases. Record the handler and tool environment; schema-valid output alone is insufficient, and subset scores are not overall BFCL scores.
Held-out application documents and conversationsInclude the actual languages, layouts, page counts and output formats, plus answerable and unanswerable questions with fixed scoring rubrics. These establish relevance to the service. Add temporal frame questions only if that path is deployed; exclude audio.

These are local recommendations based on coverage of likely failure modes. The publisher's benchmark table is a set of reported quality results, not a reproduced B300 result or an acceptance floor for Red Hat exports. Freeze item IDs before evaluation, retain a separate tuning set and label any screening subset. A different benchmark version, parser, image budget or thinking policy creates a new comparison. gemma-4-31b-it-CARD.

Run record and promotion

Fill the experiment manifest using the shared model benchmark guide and protocol. Predeclare task-specific quality floors/regression limits, latency and error budgets, useful goodput improvement and per-GPU headroom. Record how paired quality differences and repeated service runs will be analysed. A threshold left unknown prevents promotion; a confidence interval crossing the useful-improvement threshold leaves the choice inconclusive.

Deliver raw quality outputs and item scores, image/processor/template hashes, effective quantization/kernel logs, local/global memory diagnostics, cancellation/recovery evidence and a decision per workload. Reject cross-image contamination, non-finite outputs, unintended truncation or unresolved protocol corruption. The HTTP/SSE result schema covers client observations; it does not validate benchmark scoring, multimodal quality or exact token timing. No result is currently measured.

companies/mistral-ai/mistral-medium-3.5/architecture.md

Mistral Medium 3.5: architecture

Data flow

Text / Pixtral vision → projector → 88 dense GQA blocks with YaRN → output head → Mistral encoding/tool/reasoning protocol.

How the parts work together

The language network uses dense feed-forward blocks and grouped-query attention. Many query heads share a smaller set of key/value heads. Unlike the hybrid models in this catalog, its text configuration does not declare a sliding window; full token history therefore drives attention-cache growth across the language layers.

The positional configuration extends a 4,096-position reference using YaRN with factor 64. The publisher identifies a concrete correction in commit c4be198050fb5789774a55b92ed697becfbf20ae: mscale_all_dim changed from 1.0 to 0.0. The pinned base config contains 0.0. The publisher warns that derivatives built with the earlier config can inherit degraded long-context behavior. mistral-medium-3.5-FIXCFG

The Pixtral vision encoder and multimodal projector process image inputs. Their precision exclusions are part of the official FP8 export, so the whole checkpoint is not homogeneous FP8. The text architecture class, vision architecture and tokenizer/encoding stack together define a valid model load.

The official repository contains both consolidated-format and Transformers-style weight shards. These are alternate representations, not six disjoint pieces of one larger model. Downloading both layouts approximately doubles weight download/storage volume. Startup transfer depends on which layout the loader reads; retaining both on disk does not imply loading both into GPU memory.

The architecture facts above are drawn from the publisher card and configuration; the workload consequences are analytical interpretation. mistral-medium-3.5-CARD mistral-medium-3.5-CFG

This is a selected, normalized projection, not a byte-for-byte copy of the complete config. Field labels have been made comparable across models. Layer indices explicitly state zero-based or one-based conventions.

Memory and performance consequences

At the pinned revision, each of the Transformers and consolidated indexes reports metadata.total_size = 133605834656 bytes: about 133.606 decimal GB or 124.430 GiB of tensor payload per alternative layout. The sum across both alternatives is 267.212 GB and must not be used as the weight size of one loaded model. Index payload sizes exclude safetensors headers, auxiliary files and runtime allocations. mistral-medium-3.5-HF-INDEX mistral-medium-3.5-NATIVE-INDEX

For one 262,144-token sequence, separate BF16 keys and values give 2 × 88 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 elements × 2 bytes × 262144 tokens = 94,489,280,512 bytes = 88 GiB across the model. At 32,768 tokens the same ideal element payload is 11 GiB. These calculations exclude padding, any head replication, cache scales and engine overhead. FP8 KV would halve the element payload if supported and validated; quantized weights do not automatically imply FP8 KV.

A single B300 can plausibly accommodate the FP8 weights and a constrained short-context workload, but this is not a long-context/concurrency guarantee. Establish correctness with the publisher’s TP8 example, then compare TP2, TP4 and a constrained TP1 probe under the same workload and total GPU budget.

The numeric examples are calculations from stated dimensions and assumptions, not measured allocations. Memory mathematics explains the formulas and their limits. mistral-medium-3.5-CARD mistral-medium-3.5-CFG HW

What this report does not establish

Installed-image and B300 compatibility at the pinned corrected revision; runtime memory beyond the reported weight payload; maximum safe concurrency and best TP width; no audited NVFP4 variant. SGLang support is documented upstream, but has not been run locally.

The public artifacts do not disclose every training-data, optimization or implementation detail. This report does not fill missing details with assumptions or present a complete formal reconstruction of private training.

Decision and applicability

Proposed experiments; no GPU results. Determine how much tensor sharding this dense 128B service needs for its actual context, image and concurrency distribution, then assess speculation. Full-history GQA across 88 layers makes context/concurrency memory a central constraint. The current publisher card/config matched the atlas pin when retrieved again on 2026-10-15 UTC. The corrected Transformers config contains mscale_all_dim=0.0; an old derivative or a loader that interprets another layout incorrectly can invalidate long-context results. mistral-medium-3.5-CFG, mistral-medium-3.5-FIXCFG.

Start with the publisher-derived vLLM TP8 baseline. The TP2 probe and SGLang TP8 probe must qualify before comparison. Both probe profiles omit reasoning/tool parser flags: use an explicitly pinned and validated parser configuration for those tasks. The single audited target export is static FP8 with higher-precision exclusions; there is no audited BF16/NVFP4 comparison in this atlas. Dequantizing these files does not create an original BF16 quality reference. precision, serving.

All three profiles cap total context at 32,768 and active requests at 32. Begin with 4K/16K serialized inputs and 128/1,024 output budgets at concurrency 1 and 8; count image/template tokens and reserve room for generation. Increase active count only within measured headroom. A 32K input plus output, 128K contexts or larger queues need a separately qualified configuration. Reasoning-quality evaluation may need a larger declared output budget than the short service probe; report truncation rather than scoring a cut-off answer as completed reasoning.

An unresolved positional mapping or unintended loader fallback blocks comparison.

Run record and promotion

Follow the shared model benchmark guide, protocol and experiment manifest. Declare quality floors/regression limits, latency/error budgets, useful goodput improvement, memory reserve and analysis method before the campaign. Unknown thresholds block promotion. Randomize order and repeat paired A/B runs; an improvement interval crossing the declared useful threshold is inconclusive. Stable-versus-nightly comparisons need distinct artifacts, while speculation off/on needs the same build.

Deliver raw outputs and item scores, complete task/tool traces where applicable, tokenizer/parser/config hashes, weight-layout manifest, effective kernel/KV diagnostics, memory and cancellation evidence, and a decision per workload/mode. The HTTP/SSE result schema cannot certify semantic tool correctness, image quality, code execution or agent completion. These plans do not change the existing profiles' candidate/probe status, and no benchmark result is currently measured.

companies/moonshot-ai/kimi-k3/architecture.md

Kimi K3: architecture

Data flow

Text / vision features → KDA or gated MLA → attention-residual mixing → dense or latent MoE → repeat → output head; optional DSpark proposes → target verifies → commit accepted state.

How the parts work together

The text backbone alternates frequent Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) updates with periodic gated multi-head latent attention (MLA). KDA carries a recurrent summary forward; the MLA layers retain access to token history through compressed attention representations. This combination makes the model neither ordinary full attention everywhere nor a constant-memory model everywhere. A long conversation still consumes token-cache memory in the MLA layers.

The feed-forward path is a latent mixture of experts. Routing selects specialists, but the specialist computation is represented in a narrower latent space rather than treating every expert as a full-width dense feed-forward network. The dense prefix, shared experts, routers, normalization, and residual machinery still perform work. The number of selected experts therefore does not by itself determine end-to-end FLOPs or latency.

The configuration also exposes block attention-residual organization. Do not substitute a plain residual-add implementation simply because tensor shapes happen to agree. Likewise, SiTU is not interchangeable with a default SwiGLU activation: the checkpoint-dependent activation and scaling must survive expert dispatch, quantization, fusion, and reduction.

Image or video processing adds a vision encoder and transport path before language inference. Its memory and CPU-transfer overhead must be budgeted separately from text tokens. A text-only benchmark does not certify multimodal throughput.

The architecture facts above are drawn from the publisher card and configuration; the workload consequences are analytical interpretation. kimi-k3-CARD kimi-k3-CFG

Memory and performance consequences

The state pool is a separate concurrency limit from the MLA KV pool. Adding DCP can improve one pool without sharding the recurrent state in the same way. In a head-sharded thought experiment, 69 layers × 96 heads × 128 × 128 FP32 entries is exactly 434,110,464 bytes (414 MiB) of matrix state per sequence before convolution state, speculative snapshots, padding, and implementation-specific sharing. This is an illustrative formula, not an allocator measurement. Divide only by a parallelism dimension that the actual implementation uses to shard those heads.

Using the rounded publisher count, a hypothetical all-FP8 2.8T model needs approximately 2.8 TB (decimal) for idealized weights alone. That does not fit into the advertised 2.304 TB aggregate of eight B300 GPUs. Native MXFP4 and the mixed NVFP4 export change that conclusion, but usable KV and state capacity must still be established after loading and CUDA graph capture.

The numeric examples are calculations from stated dimensions and assumptions, not measured allocations. Memory mathematics explains the formulas and their limits. kimi-k3-CARD kimi-k3-CFG HW

What this report does not establish

Exact B300 SXM6-AC OEM topology; all-FP8 artifact availability; exact installed-image ancestry of mixed-format fixes; maximum safe long-context concurrency; native-versus-NVFP4 quality on your tools and languages; actual DSpark acceptance on your workload.

The public artifacts do not disclose every training-data, optimization or implementation detail. This report does not fill missing details with assumptions or present a complete formal reconstruction of private training.

companies/moonshot-ai/kimi-k3/dspark.md

Kimi K3: DSpark integration and B300 state budget

What the draft model actually does

The inspected vLLM K3DSparkModel uses a dense MLA draft path rather than the target's full latent MoE. Its context projection consumes selected target-layer features, while the target embedding can be aliased after draft loading. The implementation imports separate confidence and Markov heads. Draft-layer attention uses non-causal multi-token decoding; selected row-parallel output reductions are fused with subsequent RMS normalization. These observations concern the inspected implementation, not an assertion that every DSpark checkpoint has the same dimensions.

Read the pinned implementation and the engine recipe. Target features, vocabulary mapping, checkpoint revisions, cache format and engine implementation must agree. A different drafter name is not a drop-in optimization.

Analogy: the main author supplies a sketch of the argument to a faster assistant. The assistant proposes several words, but the author checks them together. Speed depends on useful proposals and cheap checking, not merely on the assistant being small.

The two named drafts are different artifacts

DraftImmutable revisionConfiguration distinction
Inferact/Kimi-K3-DSparkcf6b8244620e7ea4b0651d214f28e89eac75bed6Five dense MLA layers; target feature IDs [2, 23, 47, 71, 89]
RadixArk/Kimi-K3-DSpark3c5bac301d9cf392706189d82ed947feca6c2f0fFive full-attention layers, 64 query heads and 16 KV heads; target feature IDs [7, 23, 51, 67, 83]

These are the serialized feature IDs, not a promise of interchangeable indexing semantics across engines. Token IDs, attention layouts and positional configurations also differ. The Inferact card documents vLLM; the RadixArk card documents SGLang. Pin the appropriate draft independently of the target. Inferact config, RadixArk config.

Both cards publish acceptance measurements on named datasets, but those figures use their own sampling and aggregation definitions. They do not validate the SGLang cookbook's simulated-acceptance B300 speed rows. Inferact's peak-speed description pairs “4 × GB300” with tensor-parallel-size=16 without clarifying whether the four count is nodes; that topology needs clarification before reuse. This atlas does not use the peak number to rank engines. Inferact card, RadixArk card.

Why DCP8 does not divide all memory by eight

The SGLang cookbook describes a split between target MLA cache, recurrent KDA state and drafter cache. In its published sizing rule, target MLA token cache is divided by DCP, while the DSpark draft token cache remains replicated. Thus a small replicated cache can become significant after the larger target cache is sharded.

state_to_KV_pool_ratio =
    (ordinary_state_slots + intermediate_verify_slots) * state_slot_bytes
    / (average_input_plus_output_length
       * (target_MLA_bytes_per_token / DCP + draft_bytes_per_token))

The cookbook defines five ordinary slots for extra_buffer, four for extra_buffer_lazy, three for no_buffer, and one when radix caching is disabled, with additional scheduler-dependent adjustments. DSpark verification normally introduces block-size-plus-one intermediate states. ReplaySSM changes that allocation contract by using replay rings. These are version-specific engine semantics, not architecture constants. Read actual admission and cache-capacity logs after every change. SGLang cookbook

Current recipe versus a generic latest image

At retrieval, the SGLang cookbook specifically points the NVIDIA NVFP4 export at lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dev-kimi-k3-nvfp4. That is a mutable development tag, not a verified immutable image in this atlas. The compatibility merge is an ancestor of v0.5.21, but source inclusion does not establish the complete tested image/dependency stack. The cookbook and older card still name a development image; preserve that distinction when reconciling the documentation. Resolve the intended image to a digest and validate its actual code/dependencies before using the included candidates.

Published B300 DSpark rows use SGLANG_SIMULATE_ACC_LEN=4.5, making them controlled acceptance experiments rather than measured application acceptance. The local launcher rejects simulated-acceptance environment variables. The source's B300 measurement setup and its older launch-era text also have different dates: retain the exact measurement version and do not relabel it as current-nightly performance. SGLang cookbook

Begin with the target-only profile, then run the explicit DSpark profile with a pinned drafter and real prompts. Match thinking effort, preserve the model's expected multi-turn message fields, and test rejection rollback, cancellation, prefix hits and eviction. The producer requires the complete returned assistant message, including reasoning and tool fields, to be preserved for subsequent turns. Kimi model card

Kimi K3: precision and provenance

Interpretation

Moonshot describes MXFP4/MXFP8 quantization-aware training. The serialized config specifies MXFP4 groups of 32 and lists excluded modules; it leaves input_activations unset. That training description does not prove that every module or serving backend runs MXFP8 activations. NVIDIA describes BF16 attention in the original checkpoint. Base card, base config, NVIDIA card.

The derivative's config declares ModelOpt MIXED_PRECISION: expert weight/activation groups of 16 and separate FP8_PB_WO attention entries. NVIDIA reports an approximately 1.6 TB download. Download size is not resident GPU memory; scales, runtime repacking, caches and temporary allocations require separate accounting. Derivative config, NVIDIA card.

Runtime evidence

SGLang PR #35077 merged on 2026-08-19 and is an ancestor of the v0.5.21 tag. Its author reports a correctness run on 8×GB300 and explicitly reports no speed measurement. Release-source inclusion is established; the exact installed wheel or image and its dependency stack have not been tested here. The current cookbook still points this export to the mutable lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dev-kimi-k3-nvfp4 image. Do not repeat the older model card's blanket statement that pip SGLang cannot load it as a current release conclusion. Compatibility PR, release ancestry, cookbook.

NVIDIA also documents a patched vLLM path on 8×B300, using its bundled runtime_patches/sitecustomize.py and the mutable vllm/vllm-openai:kimi-k3 image. This is publisher-reported compatibility, not a local reproduction. The three linked upstream PRs — mixed dispatch #50617, attention support #52406 and SiTU scaling #52405 — remain open at this audit. The included generic vLLM NVFP4 profile therefore stays blocked pending an audited compatible image; the publisher's patched route is a separate option. NVIDIA instructions, #50617, #52406, #52405.

Deployment rule

Pin the target and tokenizer/processor revisions, quantization configuration, runtime commit, compatibility patch where used, and image digest together. Root BF16 metadata can coexist with quantized weights. Check serialized tensor types, scales, grouping, excluded modules, activation precision and runtime repacking; casting this checkpoint to BF16 does not reconstruct an original BF16 reference.

Compare target-only quality before changing KV precision or enabling speculation. The precision primer explains the formats; the validation ledger defines the local evidence still needed.

License provenance

The pinned base repository contains the custom Kimi K3 License. The NVIDIA card names the NVIDIA Open Model Agreement and separately links Kimi terms; its checked-in LICENSE is the Kimi K3 text. Preserve both provenance references rather than labeling the derivative solely with the base license. No model weights are bundled here. Base LICENSE, derivative LICENSE, derivative terms identification.

companies/moonshot-ai/kimi-k3/serving.md

Kimi K3: serving on 8×B300

Status: unbenchmarked local recommendations. The upstream recipes are evidence of documented support, not a benchmark of your node.

Engine and topology

Start with a single eight-GPU target. For native K3, compare SGLang TP8 at 64K context against vLLM’s model-specific recipe. For the NVIDIA derivative, prefer the SGLang mixed-format path as the initial compatibility candidate, with the FlashInfer TRT-LLM MoE runner required by its recipe. Its published DCP8 setup differs from the plain TP8 target-only profile included here. The cookbook disables symmetric memory under DCP; choose a documented topology before combining flags.

Establish target-only correctness first. Then attach the engine-specific drafter: Inferact’s MLA-native DSpark is documented for vLLM, while the RadixArk drafter is documented in the SGLang path. Tokenizer, hidden-state feature selection, target revision, drafter revision, KV precision, and speculative state rollback are one compatibility unit.

The repository includes separate target-only and DSpark profiles. It intentionally does not enable simulated acceptance. The SGLang cookbook marks some B300 rows as verified and other layouts as extrapolations; its simulated-acceptance results are capacity/performance experiments, not observed application acceptance. The published Inferact peak figure is not a measurement of your eight-B300 node, and its written hardware count and TP degree need clarification; see the DSpark audit.

kimi-k3-VR kimi-k3-GR kimi-k3-CARD HW

NVIDIA also publishes a vLLM route using a bundled runtime patch. Its existence prevents a blanket claim that this derivative is unsupported by vLLM; it does not validate the atlas’s generic vLLM profile. The precision report records the patch and still-open upstream PRs.

Experiment sequence

Sweep target-only versus 3/5/7-token drafting on real coding and multi-turn agent prompts. Measure accepted tokens, total emitted tokens, draft overhead, target verification cost, state-pool ceiling, TTFT and p95 token latency. Compare context 16K/64K/128K before attempting 1M. Test cancellation and resumption with non-empty speculative state.

First capture actual GPU memory, compute capability, peer topology and software versions with python scripts/preflight.py. Then verify local metadata against the immutable revisions in model.json, inspect the rendered profile and run the target-only correctness suite. Profiles live in profiles.

Acceptance gates

A successful load is necessary but insufficient. Require valid streaming framing, finite outputs, correctly separated reasoning, valid tool calls where supported, repeatable quality tests, bounded memory at load, and correct cache/state behavior after cancellation. Only then compare latency and throughput.

For production, place one sharded model process group inside a pod that owns its whole GPU group. Do not make eight independent KServe replicas and expect them to form TP8. Start with colocated prefill and decode; adopt disaggregation only after it wins the workload comparison and state transfer is correct. KS KSLLM

Parameters are not magic constants

The profile’s context cap is an application policy. Tensor parallelism is a starting layout. Memory utilization reserves room for non-weight allocations; changing it can trade cache space against startup headroom. Batch-token and sequence caps trade prefill efficiency against memory and queueing. Speculative depth trades draft/verification cost against naturally accepted tokens. Each must be varied one at a time before interaction testing.

Remaining uncertainty

Exact B300 SXM6-AC OEM topology; all-FP8 artifact availability; exact installed-image ancestry of mixed-format fixes; maximum safe long-context concurrency; native-versus-NVFP4 quality on your tools and languages; actual DSpark acceptance on your workload.

Kimi K3: validation and benchmark plan

All GPU and quality experiments below are proposed, not measured. The metadata audit was performed on 2026-10-15 (UTC). For this plan, the publisher's current and pinned cards/configs were retrieved again at 2026-10-15 22:51 UTC: the base, NVIDIA export and both named draft revisions still match model.json and sources. The base revision is f831ab66814297da540d832a5235f8e904f29d06.

Application correctness and qualityThe scored suites and experiments below remain to be run

What needs a decision

Determine whether each exact export and serving configuration preserves useful coding, tool and image quality while meeting the application's latency and capacity requirements on the same eight GPUs. The earlier instruction to sweep context and draft length did not identify a scorer, a matched target-only control, or which memory pool could cause a failure. The stages below make those distinctions observable. Use the shared benchmark selection guide, protocol and experiment record for dataset pins, paired uncertainty, request IDs and predeclared thresholds.

Applicability before timing

Campaign armStarting pointWhat must qualify first
Native MXFP4 target-onlyvLLM TP8 and SGLang TP8, both capped at 65,536 tokensExact target/tokenizer/processor pins, KDA and gated-MLA kernels, SiTU scaling, attention-residual implementation and effective weight/cache/state dtypes. Native is the available reference export; it is not an unquantized BF16 reference.
NVIDIA mixed export, target-onlySGLang candidateConfirm the mixed-format loader and required flashinfer_trtllm MoE path in the selected build. The export changes experts and selected attention projections; any quality delta belongs to that complete export.
NVIDIA mixed export on vLLMGeneric profile remains blockedAudit a compatible immutable image and any bundled patch before creating a separate run record. NVIDIA's patched route is a publisher-documented candidate, not permission to execute the blocked generic profile.
DSparkSGLang candidate; vLLM's documented Inferact routeQualify the target first, then the engine-specific draft, target feature selection, token IDs and state restoration. RadixArk and Inferact drafts have different attention layouts and target feature IDs; do not exchange them between engines.

These requirements follow the base configuration, NVIDIA export instructions and draft provenance. The hypothetical all-FP8 entry has no selected artifact and is excluded. Resolve a release, main build or nightly to its own identity using the engine roadmap; a newer tag does not qualify an export automatically.

Choose scored workloads for Kimi

Freeze item IDs, evaluator and adapter commits, sampling, reasoning effort, output extraction and generation limits before comparing engines or exports. Keep raw complete messages, including reasoning and tool fields, for the next turn. Kimi always reasons; its card requires preserved assistant history and offers low, high and max effort. A harness that drops reasoning_content is an adapter failure. kimi-k3-CARD.

Suite / proposed useWhy it is useful hereScoring and controls
Frozen LiveCodeBench code-generation release and date rangeExecutable code checks can expose precision or speculative regressions hidden by a fluent answer. Coding also supplies realistic draft acceptance.Use the official tests and declared pass@1 attempt policy; save code extraction, reasoning/output counts, timeouts and truncation. Fix evaluator runtime and resource limits. Use a common endpoint adapter or the custom-output evaluator, rather than allowing the harness to launch a different default engine. This is code generation, not a repository-agent score. MB-LIVECODEBENCH
BFCL simple_python, parallel and multi_turn_base, plus local deterministic tool fixturesExercises parser boundaries and the full reasoning/tool history contract before long agent sessions.Score tool choice/arguments and completed task separately from valid JSON. Validate the model handler preserves history. Fix tool implementations and results; log retries and every turn. The chosen category scores are not an overall BFCL score. MB-BFCL
RULER v1 plus held-out repository/document questions with known evidenceKDA recurrent state and MLA history may fail differently as length, reuse and eviction change. A single needle does not cover this.Use the official rulerv1-ns route at the cited commit and pin its NeMo-Skills dependency before running; do not use the deprecated main-branch scripts. Freeze generated examples/seeds using the Kimi tokenizer. Report per-task and per-length scores, then application answer/evidence accuracy with distractors and unanswerable questions. Synthetic success is not a 1M-context service claim. MB-RULER-V1
MMMU-Pro standard(10 options) and vision, after the image endpoint qualifiesExercises MoonViT processing and visual reasoning omitted by text-only export tests.Score the two settings separately with the official evaluator. Pin image bytes, resolution policy, image-token mapping/order and processor. Start without Python/tool augmentation; add application screenshot/document fixtures for capabilities MMMU-Pro does not isolate. Do not compare this score with a tool-augmented publisher column. MB-MMMU-PRO

Use a small fixed subset to qualify adapters, then the preselected held-out set to decide promotion. Include the application's languages and ordinary/open-ended conversations in the service trace; a coding-only acceptance figure cannot predict their drafting cost. Optional repository-agent evaluation follows endpoint qualification and needs a fixed agent scaffold, tools and task budget as described in the shared guide.

Run the experiments in this order

IDControlled experiment and mechanismRequired observations and decision
K01 — export and engine qualificationOn one engine, qualify native target-only, then the NVIDIA export with equal effective cache/state settings and topology where supported. Separately compare engines on the same export.Save resolved kernel/loader choices, module dtypes, load/repacking/graph peaks and scored text outputs. Check image quality for each qualified export. If effective paths cannot match, label a complete-configuration comparison. Reject unexpected fallbacks or task/protocol regressions before speed ranking.
K02 — recurrent state and prefix reuseReplay the same sessions cold, with a repeated prefix, after eviction, and after a cancelled request. Interleave unrelated sessions and prefixes sharing text but differing in image or tool content. Exercise prefixes on both sides of the installed cache-match boundary.Compare task outcomes and subsequent-turn state with a clean recomputation. Record KDA state slots, convolution/snapshot allocation, MLA cache occupancy, prefix hits and eviction. Reuse must not introduce another session's content or change tool state. A low-load pass alone does not qualify saturated pools.
K03 — DCP and pool allocationCompare documented TP8 without DCP against TP8/DCP8 target-only, then adjust the state-to-KV allocation in separate runs using measured demand. Keep dtype and admitted work fixed where possible.Log per-rank cache/state capacity, actual backend changes, communication time, admission stalls and peak memory. DCP shards target MLA KV; it does not imply every allocation is divided by eight. A capacity gain is useful only if quality and service objectives pass.
K04 — natural DSpark and rollbackWithin a qualified topology, compare no draft with the matching draft at its documented default. Sweep 3/5/7 proposals only where that exact implementation supports them. Change ReplaySSM policy separately where both paths are supported.Measure native acceptance distribution, its denominator, draft and verification time, extra memory, TTFT, first-final-answer latency and end-to-end task success. Include EOS/stop inside a proposed block, rejection, cancellation, eviction and the next request. If a matched off/on control cannot run, report a complete-stack comparison rather than a DSpark-only speedup.
K05 — cache/state precisionAfter K01–K04 qualify, vary supported MLA KV precision; separately vary KDA state precision with the target export fixed.Repeat long-context and reuse quality strata and record actual kernels. A smaller state dtype can also switch the verification kernel, so report that interaction. Reject a memory saving that exceeds any declared task-regression limit.
K06 — mixed load and schedulingReplay the frozen short/long/tool workload under the qualified configuration. Vary one supported admission, chunked-prefill or graph setting at a time, then confirm selected combinations.Measure offered/completed load, queue delay, p95/p99 latency, failures, task success and full-node goodput. Confirm the selected candidate on held-out sessions with cache churn; include cold/warm startup if it affects the deployment decision.

The current SGLang DSpark profile adds DCP8 and ReplaySSM as well as drafting to its target-only profile. Those two files alone cannot isolate speculative speedup. Build the supported target-only DCP control in the run manifest first, and retain any automatic backend changes. The cookbook's pool model separates KDA state, target MLA KV and replicated RadixArk draft KV; check actual allocator diagnostics instead of inferring capacity from weight size or the illustrative 414 MiB state matrix. DCP also has a documented symmetric-memory restriction. kimi-k3-GR, architecture memory explanation, DSpark audit.

The current cookbook also names a separate DFLASH route using modal-labs/Kimi-K3-DFlash, with block size 8, validation limited to Blackwell and no pipeline parallelism or DP-attention support. Treat this as a deferred candidate: it has no audited atlas artifact/profile. Pin and audit its draft revision, target/export compatibility and exact engine build before adding a matched target-only versus DFLASH experiment. Reuse K04's natural-acceptance and rollback checks; the cookbook description does not establish a local quality or speed result. kimi-k3-GR.

Length, load and reasoning budget

Start with 4K, 16K and 32K serialized input buckets at concurrency 1 and 8, then 32 and an offered-rate ladder around saturation. Here K means 1,024 tokens. The current 65,536-token cap must cover input, retained history, tool/image tokens and the reserved output together. A nominal 64K input plus generation is infeasible; record it as such or choose a smaller near-cap input explicitly. Qualify a raised cap before 64K/128K input tests, and qualify those before any 1M attempt.

Use 128/1,024 output-token shape tests only to diagnose prefill/decode interference. They may truncate Kimi's reasoning and therefore do not establish answer quality. For the quality suites, predeclare a sufficient budget from a separate pilot, keep effort and sampling fixed for A/B, and report budget exhaustion and time to a useful final answer. Compare low/high/max effort as a separate application tradeoff, not as an engine speed difference. Do not force output length or use simulated acceptance in natural DSpark runs.

Interpret published claims and produce a decision

Moonshot's benchmark table uses its stated effort, sampling, tools and harnesses. NVIDIA's native-versus-mixed-export table is publisher evidence, not a local threshold or proof of parity. The SGLang B300 DSpark speed rows use simulated acceptance; the two draft cards define their acceptance measurements differently. None supplies this campaign's natural acceptance or eight-B300 goodput. Inferact's hardware-count/TP16 wording still needs clarification. Base card, NVIDIA card, DSpark evidence.

Produce one decision row per export/topology/draft tuple with artifact identities, per-suite and critical-stratum scores, paired uncertainty, raw response/tool traces, truncation/error counts, acceptance counters, peak memory and latency/goodput at each load. An answer-retaining evaluator is required: the atlas streaming probe checks completion but does not retain answers for scoring. Promote only when predeclared quality and service limits pass; reject a demonstrated regression; mark unsupported paths blocked and unresolved comparisons inconclusive. Preserve failures and the baseline for rollback. No production SLA or numerical quality margin is supplied by this plan.

Remaining uncertainty

Exact OEM topology; all-FP8 artifact availability; image/kernel/patch provenance; usable long-context concurrency; native-versus-NVFP4 quality; natural DSpark acceptance. Inferact’s peak card also needs clarification of its hardware-count versus TP16 wording.

Use the result schema for the probe's records and the experiment/quality manifests for scored campaigns. Empty results mean not measured.

companies/z-ai/glm-5.3/architecture.md

GLM 5.3: architecture

Data flow

Tokens → dense prefix → MLA latent cache + DSA index selection → routed/shared experts → repeat → output; optional MTP → target verification.

How the parts work together

The configuration describes MLA with a separate sparse-attention indexer. The model first constructs representations that make token-history storage cheaper than retaining a separate full key/value vector for every query head. The indexer then selects a limited subset of history for the more expensive attention operation. Compression of what is stored and sparsification of what is read are distinct optimizations.

A dense prefix is followed by routed MoE layers. Shared experts provide a common feed-forward contribution while selected routed experts specialize the token transformation. The router uses its own numerical precision and score function; expert quantization is not permission to quantize router decisions without validation.

The index-selection frequency exposes reuse across layers. Reusing index selections can avoid repeated work, but correctness depends on the implementation’s layer boundaries and index cache. It is not equivalent to asking every layer to select a fresh arbitrary top-k set.

The multi-token-prediction (MTP) extension can propose multiple steps for speculative serving. It does not convert the main model into a dense small model. Generation remains a target-model process with draft verification and cache bookkeeping.

The architecture facts above are drawn from the publisher card and configuration; the workload consequences are analytical interpretation. glm-5.3-CARD glm-5.3-CFG

This is a selected, normalized projection, not a byte-for-byte copy of the complete config. Field labels have been made comparable across models. Layer indices explicitly state zero-based or one-based conventions.

Memory and performance consequences

The parameter scopes can now be reconciled. The pinned official FP8 and BF16 Hub metadata each report 753,329,940,480 parameters. The BF16 index maps 791 tensors to the extra layer model.layers.78; HTTP range reads of their five safetensors headers give 9,952,920,576 parameters. Subtracting that MTP layer gives 743,377,019,904 main-model parameters, consistent with the recipe's approximate 743B headline. The 39B active figure remains a recipe headline, not an independently counted active path. This reconciles named tensors in the stored artifacts; it does not independently verify unique training parameters, deduplicate tied/shared weights or constitute a complete tensor census. glm-5.3-META glm-5.3-BF16-INDEX Header retrievals

The FP8 index reports 755,617,140,416 serialized tensor bytes (755.62 decimal GB); the BF16 index reports 1,506,659,919,872 bytes (1,506.66 GB). These include the stored checkpoint's precision mix and are not CUDA load measurements. Both payloads are below the reference node's advertised 8 × 288 GB aggregate capacity, but per-rank allocation, KV/indexer caches, graph capture, temporary buffers and desired concurrency determine whether a launch works. A lower scheduling limit alone does not prove that one maximum-length request fits. glm-5.3-INDEX glm-5.3-BF16-INDEX

The numeric examples are calculations from stated dimensions and assumptions, not measured allocations. Memory mathematics explains the formulas and their limits. glm-5.3-CARD glm-5.3-CFG HW

What this report does not establish

Actual per-rank load and cache capacity on this node; exporter-specific quality under the application prompts; inclusion of required fixes in the selected image; and the workload crossover between vLLM and SGLang remain unmeasured. The 743B/753B accounting is now reconciled from pinned metadata.

The public artifacts do not disclose every training-data, optimization or implementation detail. This report does not fill missing details with assumptions or present a complete formal reconstruction of private training.

GLM 5.3: precision and provenance

All four artifacts below were checked at immutable revisions on 2026-10-15. A reviewed card/config is evidence of the serialization contract, not proof of successful GPU execution.

VariantPinned artifactPrecision contract from configurationIndex tensor bytes
fp8zai-org/GLM-5.3Block FP8 E4M3, 128×128 weight blocks, dynamic activations, explicit exclusions755,617,140,416
bf16zai-org/GLM-5.3-BF16BF16 reference with a small FP32 component; no quantization config1,506,659,919,872
nvfp4RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-NVFP4compressed-tensors NVFP4 W4A4 on main routed-expert linears, group size 16; MTP and other modules excluded464,824,469,712
nvfp4-inferactInferact/GLM-5.3-NVFP4ModelOpt NVFP4 on main routed experts, group size 16; MTP excluded; exporter-specific calibration metadata464,822,832,448

The byte figures are each index's metadata.total_size, not measured HBM allocations or complete repository download sizes. Full revisions and index links are in sources and model.json. The near-equal RedHat and Inferact payload sizes do not establish equal calibration or quality. RedHat explicitly excludes model.layers.78 with a regex; Inferact lists its MTP expert module among the exclusions. Thus the NVFP4 scope does not include the stored MTP expert weights.

Quality evidence

RedHat reports IFEval prompt-level strict accuracy of 85.70% for NVFP4 versus 89.77% for its local FP8 baseline, a 4.07 percentage-point difference. Its evaluation uses the same harness/serving stack, FP8 KV, temperature 1.0 and 4×B200; these are exporter results, not reproduced B300 measurements. They establish that blanket lossless-quantization language is inappropriate, without isolating every source of the difference. glm-5.3-NV

Test instruction following, tool argument fidelity, retrieval and multilingual output on the application workload. Keep the reasoning effort and conversation template identical across precision variants.

Deployment rule

Pin the model, tokenizer/processor, quantization config, engine commit and container digest together. A BF16 root dtype can coexist with quantized tensors. Serialized tensor types, scales, grouping, exclusions, activation precision and loader repacking jointly determine the execution contract. Casting an FP8 checkpoint to BF16 does not recover the original BF16 weights.

Establish target-only quality before adding lower-precision KV or speculation. Precision primer explains the format distinctions.

License provenance

The pinned publisher file is titled GLM-5.3 License. Record it as a custom license and inspect its conditions for the intended use; do not infer terms from another GLM release. The RedHat card identifies the same license name. No model tensor payloads are bundled here. glm-5.3-LICENSE

companies/z-ai/glm-5.3/serving.md

GLM 5.3: serving on 8×B300

Status: unbenchmarked local recommendations. The upstream recipes are evidence of documented support, not a benchmark of your node.

Engine and topology

Use vLLM FP8 TP8 with a deliberately capped 64K application context as the first target-only comparison. Compare TP4 for NVFP4 against TP8: four-way tensor parallelism could leave room for two independent four-GPU replicas, but only if each process really fits with the desired workload and no overlapping GPU assignment.

Add the MTP profile after the non-speculative baseline passes. The recipe’s five speculative tokens are a documented candidate, not a measurement on this node. In the current SGLang cookbook, the reasoning parser resolves to glm45 and the tool-call parser to glm47; the latter parses the newer <tool_call>/<arg_key>/<arg_value> format. Use those distinct roles when checking the SGLang profile.

The official vLLM recipe contains inconsistent historical minimum-version labels. The lock file records the current release and inspected main separately rather than pretending that the recipe proves one exact minimum supported version.

glm-5.3-VR glm-5.3-GR glm-5.3-CARD HW

Experiment sequence

Compare FP8 TP8; NVFP4 TP4; NVFP4 TP8; two isolated TP4 replicas; and MTP off versus 1/3/5 proposals. Report total node goodput, not only one replica’s tokens/second. Verify the same reasoning effort and retained conversation fields. The pinned publisher template defaults to reasoning_effort=max and clear_thinking=false; the publisher recommends explicitly enabling clear_thinking for chat. Treat those choices as workload settings, not performance-free toggles.

First capture actual GPU memory, compute capability, peer topology and software versions with python scripts/preflight.py. Then resolve immutable model metadata, inspect the rendered profile and run the target-only correctness suite. Profiles live in profiles.

The included FP8 vLLM profile explicitly selects FP8 KV, while the NVFP4 profile leaves KV selection to the engine. Record the effective cache dtype and align it through a validated setting before attributing differences to weight precision; otherwise treat cache precision as a separate experimental variable.

Acceptance gates

A successful load is necessary but insufficient. Require valid streaming framing, finite outputs, correctly separated reasoning, valid tool calls where supported, repeatable quality tests, bounded memory at load, and correct cache/state behavior after cancellation. Only then compare latency and throughput.

For production, place one sharded model process group inside a pod that owns its whole GPU group. Do not make eight independent KServe replicas and expect them to form TP8. Start with colocated prefill and decode; adopt disaggregation only after it wins the workload comparison and state transfer is correct. KS KSLLM

Parameters are not magic constants

The profile’s context cap is an application policy. Tensor parallelism is a starting layout. Memory utilization reserves room for non-weight allocations; changing it can trade cache space against startup headroom. Batch-token and sequence caps trade prefill efficiency against memory and queueing. Speculative depth trades draft/verification cost against naturally accepted tokens. Each must be varied one at a time before interaction testing.

Remaining uncertainty

Actual per-rank load and cache capacity on this node; exporter-specific quality under the application prompts; inclusion of required fixes in the selected image; and the workload crossover between vLLM and SGLang remain unmeasured. The 743B/753B accounting is now reconciled. See architecture for the pinned metadata calculation.

Decision and prerequisites

Proposed campaign; no GPU results. Determine whether an exact NVFP4 export or a different topology improves eight-GPU service capacity while preserving instruction following, coding and long-context retrieval. GLM 5.3 combines MLA with sparse history selection and a large resident MoE; it does not use Flash's KDA recurrent state. Its 2,048-token index budget and selection reuse across layers motivate sparse-cache checks, while its separate MTP layer requires its own load and verification checks. Architecture, glm-5.3-CFG.

Planning evidence was refreshed on 2026-10-15 UTC (October 16 in Paris). Current publisher card/config bytes match the pinned base revision, and current repository revisions match the four artifacts in model.json. This refresh does not qualify an engine image. Copy the experiment manifest, retaining the profile's candidate/probe status, and complete the image, tokenizer/template, effective cache dtype, hardware and workload fields before execution.

Starting armApplicability gate
vLLM FP8 TP8First target-only baseline; confirm model registration, selected MLA/DSA kernels and effective FP8 KV. Record load, warmup and graph-capture peaks on every rank.
SGLang FP8 TP8Compatibility probe. Qualify its reasoning/tool parsers and align effective KV precision before interpreting an engine difference.
RedHat NVFP4 TP8Its KV dtype is automatic in the stored profile. Establish a supported matching KV setting first; otherwise label the comparison as a complete configuration change, not a weight-precision effect.
Inferact NVFP4; official BF16Separate artifacts from precision, without supplied launch profiles. Create and qualify distinct run manifests. A successful RedHat load does not qualify ModelOpt, and casting FP8 weights to BF16 does not create the BF16 reference.

Keep reasoning_effort and clear_thinking explicit. The publisher specifies max for benchmark reproduction and recommends clear_thinking=true for chat. A service experiment with lower effort is a separate quality/latency decision. Retain the serialized conversation and record reasoning tokens, final-answer tokens and time to first final answer; early reasoning output alone does not establish responsive answers. glm-5.3-CARD.

Quality workloads and why they belong

Apply the shared benchmark selection and evaluation rules, including frozen item/scorer identities, paired quality uncertainty and answer-retaining evaluation. Start coding checks with its EvalPlus functional screen, then a frozen LiveCodeBench release/date range; these scored code-generation tests precede the more expensive repository-agent campaign below. Report pass@1, execution failures and evaluator timeouts with identical language/runtime and output budgets across exports.

WorkloadProposed evaluation and rationaleEvidence boundary
Instruction constraintsRun the pinned IFEval dataset/evaluator; retain prompt-level strict accuracy as the primary metric and per-instruction failure categories. Use the same response-field extraction, template and sampling for every export.RedHat reports 85.70% versus 89.77% for its local FP8 baseline, a 4.07 percentage-point gap. Its B200 results motivate this gate; they are not reproduced B300 scores or an allowable regression. glm-5.3-NV, MBENCH-IFEVAL.
Sparse-history retrievalUse RULER v1 retrieval, variable tracking and aggregation tasks with a fixed tokenizer, seeds and generated payload hashes. Report each task/length and add held-out application document questions. This exercises distractors and distributed evidence beyond a single easy needle.Pin the current rulerv1-ns pipeline and its NeMo-Skills dependency; the old main-branch runner is deprecated. Synthetic scores do not establish application accuracy or native 1M-context usability. MBENCH-RULER-V1, MBENCH-RULER.
Coding deployment, if requiredUse SWE-bench Verified with a frozen agent harness, task images, tool permissions, turn/token/time budgets and evaluator. Screen on a declared development subset; use an untouched evaluation set for promotion. Report resolved tasks, invalid patches, tool failures and task wall time.This is an independent application evaluation, not reproduction of the publisher's Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE or in-house scores. Those use different harnesses and budgets. MBENCH-SWEBENCH.
Application protocolFreeze English/Chinese multi-turn prompts, nested JSON/tool arguments, stop strings and tool-result follow-ups with known expected outcomes. Score schema validity and semantic argument correctness separately.Parser success is distinct from task success. Retain both raw generated text and parsed responses so parser changes cannot hide quality regressions.

Quality runs need enough output budget to reach a final answer. Record truncation as a failure category; do not use a 128-token shape probe as a reasoning-quality score. Public datasets may have appeared in training, so they complement the held-out application set.

Ordered experiments

IDControlled comparison and mechanismMeasurements and decision
G53-01: exact loadQualify FP8 target-only on each engine's stable build, then a pinned candidate build with the same topology and payloads. Audit the stored main/MTP checkpoint inventory separately from resident target tensors, documented loader exclusions, repacking and kernel selection. Intentional omission of draft tensors is valid for target-only serving.Retain readiness time, per-rank resident/peak memory, effective dtypes, finite-output and parser checks. Missing required target tensors, unexplained fallback or correctness failures block timing comparisons. Require MTP residency and precision checks when qualifying the speculative arm in G53-05.
G53-02: export qualityOn one qualified engine/build and TP8 layout, compare official FP8 with RedHat NVFP4, then Inferact NVFP4 independently. Hold cache precision and sampling fixed. Add the exact BF16 reference only after a separate memory/load gate.Produce paired quality deltas and failure categories, startup memory and useful throughput. Similar export sizes do not establish equal calibration. Promote an export only if every required quality gate passes.
G53-03: DSA/cache correctnessKeep the model's index budget and layer-reuse settings fixed. Compare a fresh request with the identical logical request after prefix reuse, unrelated-session interleaving, eviction and cancellation. Probe actual backend block/chunk boundaries and histories both below and above the 2,048 selection budget; move required evidence from start to middle to end.Retain retrieval scores by evidence position, cache/indexer allocation and available reuse counters, TTFT and errors. A stale answer after eviction or cancellation is a correctness failure, even if aggregate throughput rises. Index-selection reuse is across layers, not a four-token chunking rule.
G53-04: node capacityAfter NVFP4 TP8 passes, qualify TP4 separately, then two disjoint TP4 replicas against one TP8 group using the same eight GPUs, router and offered traffic. Hold export/cache settings fixed; confirm memory headroom at the intended load.Report whole-node goodput, latency tails, rank imbalance, communication time and peak memory. Count both replicas and routing overhead. A single TP4 process's throughput is not an eight-GPU comparison.
G53-05: native MTPStart with the FP8 MTP candidate; compare speculation off with supported depths 1/3/5 on the same build, topology and sampling. Qualify MTP tensor loading, scales and effective precision for each pairing; MTP is excluded from the NVFP4 main-expert quantization scope.Record natural accepted tokens per proposal/verification step, draft and verification cost, rollback/stop behavior, memory and task quality. Measure low load and saturation; a batch-one latency gain does not establish a throughput gain.

The inspected vLLM load path explicitly skips MTP/nextn layers in the target model and delegates them to the MTP model. Preserve that distinction in both memory inventories and failure rules; check the registered load path again for the actual image. MBENCH-GLM53-TARGET-LOADER.

For service measurements, use complete serialized input buckets of 4,096, 16,384, 32,768 and 61,440 tokens with output caps of 128 and 1,024; add a 4,096-input/8,192-output coding or reasoning trace. These are proposed shapes within the current 65,536 cap, not forced answer lengths. Count reasoning and template tokens. Raising the cap toward the native maximum is a separate capacity/accuracy experiment. Screen at concurrency 1 and 8, then 32 and a fixed offered-rate ladder from a pilot; include mixed lengths and burst/recovery traffic. Record achieved lengths, EOS and length-capped responses separately.

Required outputs and promotion

Produce one manifest per arm, raw request/response records, quality scores by task/length, load and steady-state memory per rank, profiler evidence for claimed bottlenecks, and a paired decision table. Use the protocol for warmup, randomized repeated A/B runs, uncertainty, errors and goodput. The result schema covers the lightweight client's fields; it does not replace the quality and profiler artifacts.

Before running, declare the minimum quality, maximum regression, latency/error budgets, memory reserve and minimum useful improvement. Reject any correctness failure or unmet quality gate. An improvement whose uncertainty crosses the declared useful threshold is inconclusive. If the BF16 reference cannot qualify, state that the result establishes compatibility relative to the official FP8 baseline only. Empty results remain unmeasured, and failed requests stay in the denominator.

GLM 5.3 Flash

As of 2026-10-15. Publisher headline: 320B total / 18B active. Pinned checkpoint metadata: 321.32B parameters. KDA + NoPE sparse MLA + mHC; multimodal.

Flash is a different multimodal hybrid base, not merely a faster decoding option for GLM 5.3. Its combined recurrent-state and sparse-attention behavior creates different allocation and correctness requirements. glm-5.3-flash-CARD glm-5.3-flash-CFG
